chapters.title: Introduction
chapters.summary: Egypt, one of the world's oldest civilizations, was unified around 3150 BC by King Narmer. It later came under Persian, Greek, Roman, and Arab rule before being joined to the Ottoman Empire in 1517.

events.label: 3150 BC
events.text: Egypt, one of the world's oldest civilizations, was unified around 3150 BC by King Narmer.
It later came under Persian, Greek, Roman, and Arab rule before being joined to the Ottoman Empire in 1517.

events.label: 19th c.
events.text: Controlled by Britain in the late 19th century, it became a republic in 1953.

chapters.narrative: Egypt is described as one of the world's oldest civilizations, unified around 3150 BC by King Narmer [S1]. The source states that it later came under Persian, Greek, Roman, and Arab rule before being joined to the Ottoman Empire in 1517 [S1]. It also notes that Egypt was controlled by Britain in the late 19th century and became a republic in 1953 [S1]. The excerpts provide a concise summary of Egypt's political history from unification to the modern republic [S1]. As only a brief chronological overview is provided, the material reflects a limited single perspective [S1].

chapters.title: Predynastic Egypt (pre-3150 BC)
chapters.summary: There is evidence of petroglyphs along the Nile terraces and in desert oases. In the 10th millennium BC, a culture of hunter-gatherers and fishermen was replaced by a grain-grinding culture.

events.label: 6000 BC
events.text: Climate changes and/or overgrazing around 6000 BC began to desiccate the pastoral lands of Egypt, forming the Sahara.

events.label: 3150 BC
events.text: A unified kingdom was formed in 3150 BC by King Menes, leading to a series of dynasties that ruled Egypt for the next three millennia.

events.label: 2700 BC
events.text: The first two ruling dynasties of a unified Egypt set the stage for the Old Kingdom period (c. 2700–2200 BC), which constructed many pyramids, most notably the pyramid of Djoser, constructed during the Third Dynasty and the Giza Pyramids, constructed in the Fourth Dynasty.

events.label: 2040 BC
events.text: Stronger Nile floods and stabilization of government, however, brought back renewed prosperity for the country in the Middle Kingdom c. 2040 BC, reaching a peak during the reign of Pharaoh Amenemhat III.

events.label: 1650 BC
events.text: The Hyksos migrants took over much of Lower Egypt around 1650 BC and founded a new capital at Avaris.

events.label: 1550 BC
events.text: The New Kingdom (c. 1550–1070 BC) began with the Eighteenth Dynasty, marking the rise of Egypt as an international power that expanded during its greatest extension to an empire from Syria to Upper Nubia.

events.label: 525 BC
events.text: The entire Twenty-seventh Dynasty of Egypt, from 525 BC to 402 BC, save for Petubastis III and possibly Psammetichus IV, was an entirely Persian-ruled period, with the Achaemenid kings being granted the title of pharaoh.

events.label: 358 BC
events.text: After an interval of independence, during which three indigenous dynasties reigned (the 28th, 29th and 30th dynasty), Artaxerxes III (358–338 BC) reconquered the Nile valley for a brief second period (343–332 BC), which is called the Thirty-first Dynasty of Egypt, thus starting another period of pharaohs of Persian origin.

events.label: 343 BC
events.text: It fell to the Persians again in 343 BC after the last native Pharaoh, King Nectanebo II, was defeated in battle.

Sasanian Egypt (known in Middle Persian sources as Agiptus) refers to the brief rule of Egypt and parts of Libya by the Sasanian Empire, which lasted from 619 to 629, until the Sasanian rebel Shahrbaraz made an alliance with the Byzantine emperor Heraclius and had control over Egypt returned to him.

chapters.narrative: There is evidence of petroglyphs along the Nile terraces and in desert oases [S2]. In the 10th millennium BC, a culture of hunter-gatherers and fishermen was replaced by a grain-grinding culture [S2]. Climate changes and/or overgrazing around 6000 BC began to desiccate the pastoral lands of Egypt, forming the Sahara [S2]. A unified kingdom was formed in 3150 BC by King Menes, leading to a series of dynasties that ruled Egypt for the next three millennia [S2]. The excerpts provide a single archaeological and dynastic perspective on these developments [S2]. This account focuses on cultural and environmental changes preceding dynastic rule [S2].

chapters.title: Early Islamic Egypt
chapters.summary: The Byzantines were able to regain control of the country after a brief Persian invasion early in the 7th century, until 639–642, when Egypt was invaded and conquered by the Arab Islamic Empire. The final loss of Egypt was of incalculable significance to the Byzantine Empire, which had relied on Egypt for many agricultural and manufactured goods.

events.label: 7th c.
events.text: The Byzantines were able to regain control of the country after a brief Persian invasion early in the 7th century, until 639–642, when Egypt was invaded and conquered by the Arab Islamic Empire.

chapters.narrative: The Byzantines were able to regain control of the country after a brief Persian invasion early in the 7th century [S3]. This control lasted until 639–642, when Egypt was invaded and conquered by the Arab Islamic Empire [S3]. The final loss of Egypt was of incalculable significance to the Byzantine Empire, which had relied on Egypt for many agricultural and manufactured goods [S3]. The excerpts describe these events as occurring in the 7th century [S3]. The excerpts reflect only one point of view, centered on the Byzantine Empire, and do not present other perspectives [S3]. No other viewpoints are provided in the excerpts [S3].

chapters.title: Late Medieval Egypt
chapters.summary: Muslim rulers nominated by the Islamic Caliphate remained in control of Egypt for the next six centuries, with Cairo as the seat of the Caliphate under the Fatimids. With the end of the Kurdish Ayyubid dynasty, the Mamluks, a Turco-Circassian military caste, took control about 1250.

events.text: With the end of the Kurdish Ayyubid dynasty, the Mamluks, a Turco-Circassian military caste, took control about 1250.

events.label: 14th c.
events.text: The mid-14th-century Black Death killed about 40% of the population of Egypt.
The Mamluks continued to govern the country until the conquest of Egypt by the Ottoman Turks in 1517, after which it became a province of the Ottoman Empire.

events.label: 17th c.
events.text: The Greek and Coptic languages and cultures went into a steep decline in favor of Arabic culture (though Coptic managed to last as a spoken language until the 17th century and remains a liturgical language today).

chapters.narrative: Muslim rulers nominated by the Islamic Caliphate remained in control of Egypt for the next six centuries, with Cairo as the seat of the Caliphate under the Fatimids [S4]. With the end of the Kurdish Ayyubid dynasty, the Mamluks, a Turco-Circassian military caste, took control about 1250 [S4]. The mid-14th-century Black Death killed about 40% of the population of Egypt [S4]. The Mamluks continued to govern the country until the conquest of Egypt by the Ottoman Turks in 1517, after which it became a province of the Ottoman Empire [S4]. The Greek and Coptic languages and cultures went into a steep decline in favor of Arabic culture, though Coptic managed to last as a spoken language until the 17th century and remains a liturgical language today [S4]. The excerpts reflect only a single, political, ruler-centered point of view.

chapters.title: Ottoman Egypt
chapters.summary: After the 15th century, the Ottoman invasion pushed the Egyptian system into decline. The defensive militarization damaged its civil society and economic institutions.

events.label: 15th c.
events.text: After the 15th century, the Ottoman invasion pushed the Egyptian system into decline.
The brief French invasion of Egypt led by Napoleon Bonaparte began in 1798.

Muhammad Ali's primary focus was military: he annexed Northern Sudan (1820–1824), Syria (1833), and parts of Arabia and Anatolia; but in 1841 the European powers, fearful lest he topple the Ottoman Empire itself, forced him to return most of his conquests to the Ottomans.
The title for the head of state, which in 1867 had changed from pasha to khedive, was changed again to sultan.
Ismail also tried to conquer the Ethiopian Empire and was defeated twice at Gundet in 1875 and again at the Battle of Gura in 1876.

British indirect rule lasted from 1882, when the British succeeded in defeating the Egyptian Army at Tel el-Kebir in September and took control of the country, to the 1952 Egyptian revolution which made Egypt a republic and when British advisers were expelled.
In 1914, the Protectorate was made official, and the Ottoman Empire no longer had a role.
When the British exiled Zaghlul and his associates to Malta on 8 March 1919, the country arose in its first modern revolution.
The revolt led the UK government to issue a unilateral declaration of Egypt's independence on 22 February 1922.

Continued instability due to remaining British influence and increasing political involvement by the king led to the dissolution of the parliament in a military coup d'état known as the 1952 Revolution.

chapters.narrative: After the 15th century, the Ottoman invasion pushed the Egyptian system into decline, and defensive militarization damaged civil society and economic institutions [S5]. The French invasion led by Napoleon Bonaparte began in 1798 [S5]. Muhammad Ali annexed Northern Sudan, Syria, and parts of Arabia and Anatolia, but in 1841 European powers forced him to return most conquests to the Ottomans [S5]. The title for the head of state changed from pasha to khedive in 1867 and later to sultan [S5]. British indirect rule lasted from their victory at Tel el-Kebir in 1882 to the 1952 revolution that made Egypt a republic [S5]. The Protectorate was made official in 1914, ending Ottoman role [S5].

chapters.title: Republican Egypt (since 1953)
chapters.summary: On 18 June 1953, the Egyptian Republic was declared, with General Muhammad Naguib as the first President of the Republic. Naguib was forced to resign in 1954 by Gamal Abdel Nasser – the real architect of the 1952 movement – and was later put under house arrest.

events.text: On 18 June 1953, the Egyptian Republic was declared, with General Muhammad Naguib as the first President of the Republic.
Nasser assumed power as president in June 1956.
In 1958, Egypt and Syria formed a sovereign union known as the United Arab Republic.
Three years later (1970), President Nasser died and was succeeded by Anwar Sadat.
In 1973, Egypt, along with Syria, launched the October War, a surprise attack against the Israeli forces occupying the Sinai Peninsula and the Golan Heights.
Sadat made a historic visit to Israel in 1977, which led to the 1979 peace treaty in exchange for Israeli withdrawal from Sinai.
On 6 October 1981, Sadat and six diplomats were assassinated while observing a military parade commemorating the eighth anniversary of the October 1973 War.
In 2003, the Kefaya ("Egyptian Movement for Change"), was launched to oppose the Mubarak regime and to establish democratic reforms and greater civil liberties.
On 24 June 2012, the election commission announced that Mohamed Morsi had won the election, making him the first democratically elected president of Egypt.
During the months after the coup d'état, a new constitution was prepared, which took effect on 18 January 2014.

chapters.narrative: On 18 June 1953 the Egyptian Republic was declared with General Muhammad Naguib as the first President of the Republic [S6]. Naguib was forced to resign in 1954 by Gamal Abdel Nasser and was later put under house arrest, and Nasser assumed power as president in June 1956 [S6]. In 1958 Egypt and Syria formed a sovereign union known as the United Arab Republic [S6]. President Nasser died in 1970 and was succeeded by Anwar Sadat, who with Syria launched the October War in 1973 against Israeli forces occupying the Sinai Peninsula and the Golan Heights [S6]. Sadat made a historic visit to Israel in 1977 which led to the 1979 peace treaty in exchange for Israeli withdrawal from Sinai [S6]. This summary reflects only one source's perspective [S6].
